# DeadBolt local MCP bundle

This **2.0.0-rc.2 preview bundle** includes the checksum-pinned published DeadBolt 2.0.0-rc.2 executable and a dependency-free Node.js launcher. It is a separately versioned candidate; existing stable 1.x bundles keep their original engine and behavior. Use disposable integration tests before connecting real effects.

## Try read-only setup first

Install and enable the bundle with **Operator configuration left blank**. Ask your agent to call `deadbolt_get_integration_guide` with your route (`claude_desktop`, `stdio_client`, `rust` or `http`), or call `deadbolt_check_bundle` to verify the packaged engine checksum on this host. Both return structured results, output schemas and read-only annotations. No accounts, operator state or downstream server are accessed. This mode provides **no active protection**. Checksum verification detects corruption relative to packaged metadata; it is not a security audit or independent signature verification.

Supplying a configuration path switches to the actual protected downstream server: its generated tool list replaces these two setup tools. A missing, unreadable or malformed supplied file stops startup; it never silently falls back to setup. To return deliberately to setup, stop the extension, clear its setting and restart. Terminal/editor clients can run `node /absolute/bundle/server/launcher.cjs` without a configuration argument for setup, or pass the absolute configuration path for the gate.

## Configure the tool-call gate

1. Install the `.mcpb` in a client that supports local MCP bundles and Node.js 20+. The bundle contains macOS ARM64/Intel, Linux x64 and Windows x64 binaries. Linux requires a compatible glibc system; ARM Linux and ARM Windows are not included.
2. Create a private state directory outside the bundle and outside any workspace the agent can edit. On macOS/Linux, use `mkdir -m 700 /your/private/state` and keep your configuration file private. On Windows use an operator-owned directory with appropriate ACLs. Same-user malicious code can access these files; permissions do not turn the bundle into a sandbox.
3. Copy `operator-config.example.json` to your private configuration location. Replace every placeholder with an absolute path. On Windows use JSON escaped backslashes or forward slashes. Specify the executable and arguments for an MCP server you trust. No shell command string is evaluated.
4. Enter that configuration file's absolute path in the client's **Operator configuration** setting. Choose the server's actual tool names, destination tokens and irreversible tools deliberately. `tools` must be nonempty. Every routed tool needs a discovered destination from `destinations`, unless explicitly listed in the operator-owned `offline_tools` list, which defaults to empty. An empty destination list permits no declared destination. An offline exception allows omission only; a declared foreign destination still denies. Offline exceptions must be a subset of allowed tools and are recorded as Observed policy evidence. Do not exempt general code execution without independent OS egress controls. `spend_cap_usd` is a cap on application-reported amounts, not an independent billing meter.
5. Set `hard_deadline_at` to a future integer Unix timestamp, and choose `renewal_mode` deliberately: `activity` or `supervisor`. The example's zero deadline is an invalid placeholder; replace it before use. Unix seconds can be read with `date +%s`, or with Node on every supported host: `node -p "Math.floor(Date.now()/1000)"`. Add your chosen run duration in seconds.
6. Save the configuration and enable the extension in your client. In Claude Desktop, check **Settings → Developer** for a **Running** status. The launcher issues a missing run with its fixed deadline, sets your explicit policy, and checks its liveness **before starting your configured server**. Existing state must match the same deadline and renewal mode; an idle-only 1.x run is never silently upgraded. It never grants approvals, resumes a pause or clears a kill. Setup errors exit before the configured server starts. Diagnostics go to stderr; stdout remains MCP-only.

The engine's default idle TTL is 60 seconds. In `activity` mode, live admissions (including denials) renew that idle TTL, but never past the fixed deadline. In `supervisor` mode, admissions do not renew it: an independently operated supervisor must renew through the trusted sidecar using a separate renewal-only key. The launcher neither creates nor reads that key and never forwards it downstream. See the [supervisor guide](https://github.com/seanebones-lang/deadbolt/blob/main/docs/SUPERVISION.md) for operator provisioning and renewal. Choose activity mode if you have no supervisor. Silence without renewal expires either mode, and an expired lease cannot be revived by restarting this launcher. For a new run, stop the old session and choose a fresh operator-assigned agent ID. A killed ID stays killed. A fixed deadline never slides, including across restarts. Deadline or mode changes for an existing ID fail closed; issue a fresh ID deliberately. A paused run must be resumed through the operator before this launcher will start its configured child. Do not reuse one ID for concurrent sessions: the launcher applies the configuration's policy to that ID at each startup. The example uses a $10 cap on reported spend; choose your own limit. A zero cap blocks all tool admission, including requests reporting no spend.

Bundle 1.0.1 supports ordinary Node and hosted runtimes that import the entry point and bridge message streams, including Claude Desktop's built-in Node. It fixes bundle 1.0.0's startup stall in that runtime. The trusted downstream server still needs its own executable/runtime; the host's embedded Node executable is not a general-purpose Node command.

If the client says the server failed to start, inspect its developer logs and verify the private configuration, existing state directory and downstream executable. Policy denials return a tool result with `isError: true`, a short `DeadBolt denied: CODE` message and stable reason/retry metadata. `killed`, `lease_expired` and `deadline_exceeded` are final for that run; `paused` requires operator resumption before another attempt. Protocol or setup failures remain separate errors. If your host still hides the tool result, inspect local evidence or `incident --agent ID` using the configured state paths; do not guess the cause. Claude Desktop's own **Allow once** permits an attempt; it does not grant DeadBolt operator approval. Do not retry denied effects or clear a kill to hide a failure.

## Operator controls

Use the binary under `native/<your-target>/deadbolt` (`deadbolt.exe` on Windows). Set `DEADBOLT_DB` and `DEADBOLT_EVENTS` to the **same absolute paths as your configuration file**. Then use `status --agent ID`, `pause --agent ID`, `clip TOOL --agent ID`, `approve --agent ID --tool TOOL`, `kill --agent ID`, or `incident --agent ID`.

The launcher's `irreversible_tools` configuration uses broad one-shot tool approvals. Although the bundled 2.0 engine supports exact-action grants through a trusted adapter, this launcher does not configure those grants or read credential files. Do not interpret a broad `approve` as consent bound to exact recipients or arguments. Review the action in your trusted application. Operator CLI commands are not exposed to the agent as MCP tools. Keep the state, configuration and operator access under trusted control.

## Boundary

DeadBolt admits routed `tools/call` requests before they reach the child. Startup and non-tool methods (including resources and initialization) are forwarded outside that gate. The downstream server has its ordinary OS access and remains trusted. Destination discovery and reported spend are conventions described in `engine-docs/INTEGRATION.md`; custom network tools may need an executor adapter that supplies the declared destination. Destination declarations and offline exceptions are policy, not OS network enforcement. Pair them with independent egress controls when containment is required. Nothing here intercepts arbitrary network traffic, contains arbitrary code, cancels an already running tool body or makes an external action atomic with permission.

The launcher removes inherited `DEADBOLT_*` variables and sets only the configuration's state paths, so unrelated environment settings cannot select another store or inject proxy credentials. Other environment variables are inherited by the trusted server: supply only the credentials that server requires. Decision records remain local and operator-writable. This is not compliance certification.

`PROVENANCE.json` records the source revisions, published archive checksums and binary checksums. The launcher checks the selected binary against this packaged metadata before execution. This catches packaging corruption; it is not a signature against an attacker who can edit the whole bundle. macOS binaries retain their original Developer ID signatures; Linux and Windows releases are unsigned. The outer bundle is not signed.

In configured mode the bundle's tools come from your trusted downstream server. In blank-configuration mode only the two built-in read-only setup tools are exposed. No downstream server is bundled. Local acceptance tests use disposable fixture tools, not your accounts, files or credentials. See the distribution acceptance report for actual tested platforms; including a platform's binary does not prove this wrapper was tested on that platform.

Source: https://github.com/seanebones-lang/deadbolt

Captioned demonstration: https://huggingface.co/spaces/Nextleven/deadbolt

## Upgrade from a 1.x bundle

Stop the old client connection first. Keep its operator database and evidence; do not delete state to bypass a denial. Create a version **2** configuration with a fresh agent ID, a fixed future `hard_deadline_at`, an explicit `renewal_mode`, and reviewed `offline_tools` (empty unless deliberately granted). Version 1 configuration is refused rather than interpreted with changed destination semantics. Old killed/expired runs remain in the database; no approvals are transferred to a fresh run. Keep the original 1.x bundle available if you need its supported compatibility path. The engine performs its documented database migration; consult the [2.0 migration guide](https://github.com/seanebones-lang/deadbolt/blob/main/docs/MIGRATING-V2.md) and back up private state before upgrading.

The fixed deadline bounds **new admissions**, not already running work. Client disconnection and process cleanup do not provide the owned process-group cancellation guarantee described by the separate POSIX executor helper.
